title: A General Framework for Uncertainty Estimation in Deep Learning
abstract: Neural networks predictions are unreliable when the input sample is out of the training distribution or corrupted by noise. Being able to detect such failures automatically is fundamental to integrate deep learning algorithms into robotics. Current approaches for uncertainty estimation of neural networks require changes to the network and optimization process, typically ignore prior knowledge about the data, and tend to make over-simplifying assumptions which underestimate uncertainty. To address these limitations, we propose a novel framework for uncertainty estimation. Based on Bayesian belief networks and Monte-Carlo sampling, our framework not only fully models the different sources of prediction uncertainty, but also incorporates prior data information, e.g. sensor noise. We show theoretically that this gives us the ability to capture uncertainty better than existing methods. In addition, our framework has several desirable properties: (i) it is agnostic to the network architecture and task; (ii) it does not require changes in the optimization process; (iii) it can be applied to already trained architectures. We thoroughly validate the proposed framework through extensive experiments on both computer vision and control tasks, where we outperform previous methods by up to 23% in accuracy. The video available at https://youtu.be/X7n-bRS5vSM shows qualitative results of our experiments. The project's code is available at: https://tinyurl.com/s3nygw7.

claims.text: Combining Bayesian belief networks with Monte-Carlo sampling models both data uncertainty and model uncertainty for deep neural network predictions.
Input sensor noise characteristics can be forward-propagated through neural network layers via Assumed Density Filtering to quantify prediction data uncertainty.
Optimal test-time dropout rates for estimating model uncertainty in an already trained network can be determined by minimizing negative log-likelihood on ground-truth labels without re-training.
On end-to-end steering angle prediction using the Udacity dataset, the framework achieves an RMSE of 0.09, EVA of 0.81, and NLL of -1.0 without model re-training.
On object future motion prediction using the DAVIS 2016 dataset, the proposed framework achieves an endpoint error (EPE) of 5.91, KL divergence of 45.1, and NLL of 4.07.
On CIFAR-10 object recognition, the proposed framework achieves 94.0% accuracy and an NLL of 2.65.

Applying MLP model error compensation in closed-loop quadrotor control only when prediction uncertainty is below a threshold reduces trajectory tracking RMSE to 0.084 on circular and 0.234 on lemniscate maneuvers.

limitations.text: Current approaches for uncertainty estimation require architectural changes and re-training, disregard prior knowledge about data noise, or underestimate uncertainty by ignoring relationships between data and model uncertainty.

Generating total uncertainty requires multiple network forward passes per input sample, which creates computational latency and is particularly expensive for recurrent models that must unroll temporal sequences for every sample.

future_work.text: Finding alternative non-sampling solutions to compute model uncertainty, such as using information theory.
